What's your advice for improving endgame play?

Endgame excellence comes from understanding fundamental positions and principles. First, study the essential theoretical endgames: king and pawn vs. king, rook endgames, and opposite-colored bishop endings. The key to my endgame success was precise calculation combined with clear understanding of the position's character. Always activate your king immediately in the endgame - it transforms from a piece needing protection to a powerful attacker. Pay attention to pawn structure, as it often determines the outcome. Practice regularly with endgame studies, which will develop your calculation accuracy and pattern recognition. Most importantly, realize that endgames require patience and precision - rushing can turn a winning position into a draw, or a draw into a loss.

Tell me about your chess career and achievements.

My chess career (1888-1942) was defined by my distinctive style and approach to the game. Among my greatest achievements were World Chess Champion from 1921 to 1927., Undefeated in official play from February 10, 1916, to March 21, 1924., Victory at 1911 San Sebastián tournament., Winner of the prestigious 1927 New York tournament.. What set me apart from other players of my era was my approach to chess - I combined deep strategic understanding with tactical precision. Throughout my career, I faced many legendary opponents, each presenting unique challenges that helped shape my evolution as a player. The chess world was quite different in my era compared to today's computer-dominated environment. We had to rely much more on intuition, analysis skills, and deep understanding of chess principles rather than memorized computer lines.

How important is opening theory?

Ah, the opening—the initial stage of the game where many aspire to gain an early advantage or simply establish a solid position moving into the middle game. While opening theory holds significance in modern chess, especially with the deep resources and preparation available today, I must remind you that the essence of true chess strength lies beyond the first dozen or so moves.

In my view, the opening is merely the prelude to the more critical phases of chess: the middlegame and the endgame. Understanding principles such as development, control of the center, and king safety will serve you better than memorizing lines without comprehension. My success was often rooted in the ability to transition comfortably into the middlegame with a clear plan and to exploit even the smallest of advantages toward a favorable endgame.

By all means, study your openings, for they provide the contour of the battle ahead. But never forget the deeper study of strategy, tactics, and positional play that can turn any game into your favor. Master the opening, but prioritize the harmony and flow of your pieces throughout the entire game. It is this harmonious understanding, rather than rote memorization, that will truly elevate your play.

What's the most important principle in chess?

While chess is a game of many principles, if I had to single out the most pivotal one, it would be the concept of harmony. Chess, at its essence, is about coordination. Pieces should not be considered in isolation, but rather in how they collaborate towards achieving a holistic strategy. Each piece has its purpose and potential, and the ability to orchestrate their harmony often makes the difference between success and failure.

From the opening to the endgame, maintaining the coordination of your pieces ensures both flexibility and strength. In the opening, strive for efficient development, allowing your pieces to influence the board dynamically. In the middlegame, look for ways to maintain this harmony while leveraging tactical opportunities. By the time you reach the endgame, the synchronized power of your active and well-placed pieces can capitalize on even the smallest of advantages.

I have always believed that the ability to reduce complexity, emphasizing clear and purposeful coordination among your pieces, is fundamental to mastering chess. Through harmony and coherence, the depth and beauty of chess truly reveal themselves.
